title: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: when any part or organ is repeated many times in the structure of the same individual (as the vertebræ in snakes, and the stamens in polyandrous flowers) the number is variable; whereas the number of the same part or organ, when it occurs in lesser numbers, is constant.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Multiple, rudimentary, and lowly organised structures variable.”. Scope: plants and animals with serially repeated parts

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Repeat count and within-species variance are direct variables with a clear comparative prediction. Individual-level replication is too sparse for broad plant-and-animal coverage.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across species, estimate within-species variance in part number and regress it on mean repeat number, comparing serial structures with low-copy homologues. A robust positive relationship and near constancy at low copy number support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Repositories emphasize species representatives rather than within-species samples.

Developmental constraints differ among structure types.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.79
data adequacy: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.66
data existence: 0.63
operationalizability: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The rule is a comparison of coefficients of variation and needs little reinterpretation. Fishes and some floral traits are already in public tables, while snakes, many plants, and other repeated organs still require monograph compilation. Within the coded groups the contrast is discriminating if sample size is handled explicitly, and that compilation is the main delay.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare coefficients of variation in counts of many-times-repeated parts, such as vertebrae or stamens, with counts of parts that occur in small numbers. A decline in variability as the typical count declines would confirm the rule; similar coefficients after equalizing sample size would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Museum counts and trait databases use inconsistent sample sizes.

Low-count parts are often defined as invariant, which can bake in the pattern.

Within-species count variances are incomplete outside fishes and a subset of flowers.
